title: Govt removes Dan Bahadur Karki as Nepal Police chief, appoints him adviser to PM’s Office - OnlineKhabar English News
description: Govt removes Dan Bahadur Karki as Nepal Police chief, appoints him adviser to PM’s Office  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
Kathmandu, November 4

The government has removed Dan Bahadur Karki from the post of Inspector General of Police (IGP), transferring him to the Prime Minister’s Office as an adviser.

A Cabinet meeting decided to relieve Karki of his responsibilities as police chief and place him under the Prime Minister’s Office in an advisory role.

The government’s decision comes amid allegations that Karki played a role in a series of controversial recent incidents.

The Cabinet opted to transfer him to the Prime Minister’s Office rather than dismiss him outright, as a direct removal was likely to invite legal complications.

The government has decided to appoint AIG Manoj KC as the new IGP.

Karki was appointed IGP by the government led by Sushila Karki on November 10, 2025. He assumed office on November 12. During the Gen Z protests on September 9, he was in charge of the Kathmandu Valley command.

His tenure of around a year was marked by several controversies. He faced allegations of irregularities in the procurement of uniforms for election police, while the government also questioned his command and control.

He was also criticised for allegedly running the police command in accordance with instructions from individuals close to the prime minister.

Last week, police were deployed to media offices and journalists’ homes, leading to arrests and detentions. It later emerged that Karki had allegedly ordered the operations at the direction of individuals in the Prime Minister’s Secretariat.

He was also criticised for complying with instructions to carry out arrests, including those alleged to be unlawful. Courts subsequently ruled that some of the arrests were illegal.

title: Who is Manoj KC, the officer now leading Nepal Police? - The Kathmandu Post
description: Who is Manoj KC, the officer now leading Nepal Police?  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The Cabinet on Wednesday assigned Additional Inspector General Manoj KC to lead Nepal Police after removing Inspector General Dan Bahadur Karki at an emergency meeting. KC had been heading the Crime Investigation Department at Nepal Police headquarters.

On September 21, 2025, the government transferred KC from the Police Provincial Coordination Department to the Central Investigation Bureau (CIB). He was later moved to the Crime Investigation Department.”

When Karki was appointed inspector general, KC was among three additional inspector generals in contention for the top police post. The other contenders were Rajan Adhikari and Siddhi Bikram Shah.

Karki, Adhikari and KC joined the police service as inspectors in 1998, making KC a contemporary of Karki from the same recruitment cohort.

KC came into prominence for his role in advancing the investigation into the fake Bhutanese refugee scam while heading the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office.

The case had remained stalled for a long time before KC moved forward with a complaint and arrested three suspects on March 26, 2023. They were Keshav Dulal, Tanka Gurung and Sanu Bhandari, members of a racket that allegedly sent Nepali youths to the United States by passing them off as Bhutanese refugees. Their arrests gave fresh momentum to the investigation.

The investigation later expanded to include organised crime charges, leading to the arrests of several high-profile figures, including former Home Minister Bal Krishna Khand, former deputy prime minister Top Bahadur Rayamajhi and then home secretary Tek Narayan Pandey.

KC was a senior superintendent of police (SSP) when the fake refugee scam came to light. A team under his command went to the residence of Nepali Congress leader Khand to arrest him.

The operation angered the Nepali Congress leadership. KC did not receive key postings while the party remained in government.

title: Ramanan: Socso to pay RM174,000 in benefits to families of 28 Nepal-Tibet flood victims - Malay Mail
description: Ramanan: Socso to pay RM174,000 in benefits to families of 28 Nepal-Tibet flood victims  Malay Mail
publisher.title: Malay Mail
full_article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 4 — Twenty-eight out of the 54 victims of the flood tragedy in the Nepal-Tibet region on August 26 met the contribution eligibility requirements of Social Security Organisation (Socso), thereby entitling their next-of-kin to receive benefits.

Human Resources Minister Datuk Seri R. Ramanan said the total payout, amounting to RM174,000, includes an immediate financial aid of RM3,000 as well as a Survivors’ Pension under the Invalidity Scheme, which has been disbursed to the families of the affected victims.

“Today, 16 families (out of the 28 eligible families) are present. I understand that, to this day, these families continue to face uncertainty regarding the fate of their loved ones. I am well aware that no form of assistance can truly alleviate such deep anxiety.

“Nevertheless, on behalf of the government, I do not want these families especially those who have lost their primary breadwinner to bear this burden alone. Therefore, the Ministry of Human Resources (Kesuma), through Socso, has strived to ensure that the eligible next-of-kin receive appropriate protection and support,” he said.

He made these remarks during a press conference held today at the PERKESO Tower in Kuala Lumpur, regarding the disbursement of Socso benefits to the victims of the Nepal floods. Also present were Socso board chairman Datuk Seri Subahan Kamal and Socso group chief executive officer Datuk Seri Dr. Mohammed Azman Aziz Mohammed.

Ramanan noted that Socso has conducted a thorough review to ensure that no eligible next-of-kin is overlooked or excluded from receiving the necessary protection.

“The pension disbursement process will be carried out as soon as all relevant information and documentation are complete. For victims who do not have a record of Socso contributions, please know that we remain deeply concerned and attentive to the plight of your families.”

“Through the Social Synergy Programme, Socso will help connect affected families with 990 strategic partners including 130 agencies nationwide to identify other suitable forms of assistance to help ease their burden,” he said. — Bernama

title: Out as IGP, in as adviser: Nepal has seen this before - The Kathmandu Post
description: Out as IGP, in as adviser: Nepal has seen this before  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The Rastriya Swatantra Party-led government’s removal of Dan Bahadur Karki as inspector general of police has revived memories of a similar episode three decades ago.

Less than a month after becoming home minister, Bamdev Gautam removed then IGP Achyut Krishna Kharel and installed an IGP of his own choosing. On April 3, 1997, with Kharel having spent just 36 days in office, Gautam transferred him to head the Investigation Department.

A newspaper clipping from April 1997 reports Dhruba Bahadur Pradhan’s appointment as IGP after Home Minister Bamdev Gautam removed Achyut Krishna Kharel. From Kantipur archives

Gautam appointed then additional inspector general Dhruba Bahadur Pradhan as the new IGP. Govinda Thapa, the Investigation Department chief, was shifted to the Special Police. The decision drew widespread criticism.

Kharel, claiming he had been removed illegally, petitioned the Supreme Court for reinstatement. Eight months later, the court did not issue a ruling. Hearings were held, but no verdict came.

Gautam himself was under fire at the time. The opposition accused him of misusing state machinery to defeat their candidates in the local elections held after he became home minister, and demanded an investigation.

Kharel was removed during Lokendra Bahadur Chand’s prime ministership. But the Chand government collapsed on October 7, 1997, and Surya Bahadur Thapa became prime minister with Nepali Congress support. His cabinet restored Kharel as IGP and appointed Pradhan as special adviser to the prime minister. It also reinstated Thapa as chief of the Investigation Department.

A clipping from late 1997 reports Achyut Krishna Kharel’s reinstatement as IGP under the Surya Bahadur Thapa government. From Kantipur archives

The cabinet cited several grounds: the Public Service Commission had not been consulted when Special Service officers were appointed to the civil service; Kharel had been abruptly removed before completing his legally mandated tenure, and his appointment as chief of the Special Service was not lawful; and the decision had created confusion in the police force.

Resuming office at Police Headquarters on December 11, Kharel said self-serving tendencies must not be allowed to take root in the police organisation. He argued that a police officer who joins the force should be able to retire from it.

title: Who is Manoj KC, Nepal Police’s 34th IGP? - OnlineKhabar English News
description: Who is Manoj KC, Nepal Police’s 34th IGP?  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
AIG Manoj KC has become the 34th Inspector General of Nepal Police after the government relieved Dan Bahadur Karki of his duties.

On Wednesday, the Cabinet decided to promote AIG Manoj KC, head of the Crime Investigation Department, to IGP.

Karki’s tenure was due to run until April 9, 2028. The government has transferred him to the post of the Prime Minister’s special security adviser and appointed KC as IGP.

The government has removed an IGP before. In 1997, it removed Achyut Krishna Kharel as IGP and transferred him to the National Investigation Department. Kharel never reported there. He went to the Supreme Court, arguing that he had been transferred to a post that did not exist.

The government made Dhruba Bahadur Pradhan IGP in his place. After winning his case in the Supreme Court, Kharel became IGP again. The government then transferred Pradhan to the post of the Prime Minister’s special security adviser.

The government also moved Ramesh Chand Thakuri to the security adviser post. At the time, it said it was doing so because he was implicated in the Sudan scandal. Rabindra Pratap Shah was then made IGP in his place.

KC, the new IGP, is from the same batch as Karki. Both joined the police as inspectors on April 10, 1998.

KC was promoted to DSP on December 11, 2009 and to SP on August 3, 2017 BS. He became an SSP on July 19, 2022, a DIG on May 26, 2024 and an AIG on April 24, 2025.

When he was promoted to AIG, he ranked third. Karki, who has now been moved to the security adviser post, was first, and Rajan Adhikari was second. By putting Karki in the adviser’s post, the government bypassed even the second-ranked Adhikari and made KC the IGP.

KC rose to prominence for leading the investigation, as head of the Crime Investigation Office, into the fraud in which Nepali citizens were taken to the United States posing as Bhutanese refugees. By coincidence, while KC led that investigation, the case’s prosecution side was handled by Karki, who has now been removed as IGP.

KC holds a PhD in conflict transformation from Panñāsāstra University of Cambodia. He also has a master’s in applied conflict transformation studies from the same university, a master’s in sociology from Tribhuvan University and a master’s in public administration from Tribhuvan University.

KC is the founding director of the Police Staff College, the first of its kind in Nepal Police. While at the Police Academy, he developed the curriculum for a master’s programme in police science.

He has commanded the police’s Central Investigation Bureau (CIB), the Crime Investigation Department, the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office, the District Police Office in Rupandehi and several other districts.

Before joining the CIB, KC worked in the Provincial Coordination Department at police headquarters. As DIG, he worked in the Special Bureau and at the Police Academy. As SSP, he was moved from the Crime Investigation Office to the Women, Children and Senior Citizens Directorate at headquarters.

At the CIB, he led investigations into fake helicopter rescue scams in tourist areas, the Smart Telecom fraud, securities and insurance fraud, cryptocurrency crimes, and the encroachment and misappropriation of government land.

He also has experience on UN missions, having served as a security officer in the UN missions in Kosovo and Haiti. KC is fluent in French and Spanish.

Visiting Indian Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri has expressed India’s readiness to support Nepal’s efforts to rebuild infrastructure damaged by the Bhotekoshi flood , saying New Delhi is prepared to consider assistance and project proposals as the country moves into the reconstruction and rehabilitation phase.

Misri also described relations between Nepal and India as unique, saying the two countries had stood by each other in both good times and difficult circumstances. He praised officials from both countries for their continued efforts to advance bilateral cooperation, saying their work had helped resolve long-pending issues and move key initiatives forward.

Misri also thanked Rai and his team for their continued support, reiterating that Nepal and India shared a distinctive relationship built on cooperation through both favourable and difficult times.

full_article:
KATHMANDU: The Rastriya Swatantra Party-led government’s decision to remove Dan Bahadur Karki as Inspector General of Police (IGP) has brought back memories of a similar controversy in Nepal Police nearly three decades ago.

Following Wednesday’s Cabinet meeting, government Spokesperson and Minister for Education and Sports Sasmit Pokharel stated that IGP Dan Bahadur Karki had been transferred to the newly created position of Special Security Adviser to the Prime Minister, while AIG Manoj Kumar KC, who currently heads the Criminal Investigation Department, had been appointed as the new IGP.

The government and the police leadership had reportedly been at odds for some time over allegations of irregularities in the procurement of uniforms for temporary police personnel deployed during the elections.

Although the government has formally assigned Karki the role of Special Security Adviser to the Prime Minister, the decision effectively removes him from the leadership of Nepal Police, marking a significant change in the police command.

In 1997, then Home Minister Bamdev Gautam removed then IGP Achyut Krishna Kharel less than a month after assuming office and appointed a police chief of his choice. On April 3, 1997, just 36 days after Kharel took charge as IGP, Gautam transferred him to head the Investigation Department.

Gautam subsequently appointed then Additional Inspector General Dhruba Bahadur Pradhan as the new police chief. Govinda Thapa, who was heading the Investigation Department, was transferred to the Special Police. The reshuffle triggered widespread criticism.

Kharel had then challenged the decision in the Supreme Court, arguing that his removal was unlawful, and sought reinstatement. Although the court conducted hearings over the following eight months, it did not deliver a verdict.

The controversy unfolded at a time when Gautam was himself facing political pressure. Opposition parties accused him of misusing state machinery to influence the outcome of local elections held after his appointment as Home Minister and demanded an investigation into the allegations.

Kharel’s removal took place during the premiership of Lokendra Bahadur Chand. However, the Chand-led government collapsed on October 7, 1997, paving the way for Surya Bahadur Thapa to become Prime Minister with the support of the Nepali Congress.

The new government subsequently reinstated Kharel as IGP and appointed Pradhan as Special Adviser to the Prime Minister. Govinda Thapa was also restored to his previous position as chief of the Investigation Department.

The Cabinet cited several reasons for reversing the earlier decisions. These included the failure to consult the Public Service Commission before appointing Special Service personnel to civil service positions, Kharel’s premature removal before completing his legally prescribed tenure, and the alleged illegality of his appointment as chief of the Special Service. The government also said the earlier reshuffle had created confusion within the police organisation.

Kharel returned to Nepal Police Headquarters on December 11, 1997. Addressing the issue, he said personal interests and self-serving tendencies should not be allowed to influence the police organisation.

title: 'It stood like a serpent right there staring at us': American who survived deadly Nepal flood tells her story - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
description: 'It stood like a serpent right there staring at us': American who survived deadly Nepal flood tells her story  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
publisher.title: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
full_article:
KATHMANDU, NEPAL -- Anjana Raja had long dreamed of traveling to Nepal as part of a spiritual journey to Mount Kailash ever since she was a teenager, she said.

When she and her husband finally got to make that dream a reality this month, the California mom of two told ABC News she could not have imagined that trip would force them into survival mode as they found themselves nearly swept up in the deadly landslide flood that hit the region Wednesday.

Nepal survivor Anjana Raja speaks to ABC News. ABC News

Raja recalled sitting on a bus with her husband traveling to the Chinese border on Wednesday when, all of a sudden, the driver and front passengers fled the bus and she saw the landslide coming toward their vehicle.

Related Hundreds dead as over 2,000 remain missing in massive Nepal-Tibet flood

"It was water mixed with the mud that was a good 50 to 60 feet high. It stood like a serpent right there staring at us," Raja told ABC News. "Like a cobra's head staring at you."

Firefighters conduct a search and rescue operation at a damaged road leading to Gyirong Port after a mudslide, in Gyirong county, Shigatse, Tibet Autonomous Region, China, August 28, 2026. Cnsphoto via Reuters

Raja said she didn't hesitate and grabbed her sling bag and turned to her husband, Pattabiraman Venkatesan.

"I grabbed him by the collar, and I said, 'Run, we need to go right now,'" she said.

"I didn't even give time to act. I just said, 'Leave the bus right away or we're gonna die,'" Raja added.

A collapsed bridge and damaged settlements debris and mud covers an area following flash floods, August 28, 2026 in DeviGhat village, Nepal. Ritesh Shukla/Getty Images

As of Friday, as intense search and rescue efforts continue, 584 people have been reported dead in the floods, according to the Nepal National Disaster Management Authority and Chinese government.

Meanwhile, over 2,400 people were reported missing according to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority and the Chinese government.

Faced with the huge wall of water and mud, the couple and other bus passengers ran to a camp right next to the bus and made their way to higher ground as the water hit and completely flooded the streets, she said.

"We just blindly...climbed. We didn't even know what direction ... There was no guide for us, there was nobody, we were just frantically running. Running, literally running. It was slushy, it was muddy, we were climbing rocks, which was slippery. We just ran for our life," she said.

"When we reached the second level ... I saw the water come up to the slope and move our bus. I told my husband 'That's it, we're gone. We're going to die,'" she said.

They ultimately made their way up to the third level of the camp and they watched in shock as the wall of water rushed past them.

From their point they could see vehicles, objects and even people be taken in by the water's power, although the water never reached their level.

"It just came like a roar, it sucked a bunch of buses, SUVs, people, the basecamp, everything -- took it in, turned it, turned it all upside down and dumped it into the ground," Raja said.

Residents salvage belongings from their destroyed home following flash floods, August 28, 2026 in Devighat, Nepal. Ezra Acayan/Getty Images

Eventually, Raja said she and her husband were able to contact her daughter Amanda, a physician, back in California and they have been in constant contact. The couple also has a college-age son.

Related What caused Nepal flood? Scientist says it was enormous landslide, glacier fall

Raja commended the actions of first responders, especially how they worked to take care of the most vulnerable victims.

"What I really loved is his focus was not foreign nationals, nor U.S. citizens. He looked at us as humans," she said of her rescuer.

Raja said that the entire experience has left a long-lasting impression on her.

"I know time will heal but I think, with all this what happened, I think I've become stronger mentally, emotionally. I'm not crying so that's a good thing," she said.

Nepal survivor Anjana Raja speaks to ABC News. ABC News

Still, Raja said she and her husband are determined to return and complete their journey to Mount Kailash.

"I am determined to," she said.

title: From heartbleed to PHP2Shell: Is Nepal ready for the next cyber crisis? - The Annapurna Express
description: From heartbleed to PHP2Shell: Is Nepal ready for the next cyber crisis?  The Annapurna Express
publisher.title: The Annapurna Express
full_article:
In Oct 2026, thousands of government websites in Nepal suddenly disappeared from the internet. No nationwide cyberattack was confirmed. Authorities took websites and some online services offline as a precaution. The trigger was two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language widely used for websites. Known collectively as PHP2Shell, the weaknesses could allow attackers to run malicious code on certain affected servers without logging in. Fixes existed, but officials still needed to find affected systems and apply them.

Most websites were subsequently restored. But if a software flaw can interrupt public services even after a fix exists, how ready is Nepal for the next one?

A vulnerability is a weakness attackers might exploit; discovering one does not mean an attack occurred. Nor does a patch automatically protect every system. Someone must know where the software runs, who maintains it and whether attackers arrived before repairs.

The past 12 years show how often the same cybersecurity failures have resurfaced around the world.

In 2014, Heartbleed exposed a flaw in OpenSSL, software that helps protect information travelling across the internet. The flaw could reveal sensitive server-memory data, turning an invisible software component into a risk for services people trusted. That year, Shellshock exposed flaws in Bash, a command interpreter used by Unix-like systems. Under certain conditions, attackers could execute unauthorized commands. Even longstanding software was not necessarily safe.

In 2017, the consequences became visible. WannaCry ransomware spread internationally through a Windows networking vulnerability, encrypting files and disrupting essential operations.

Britain’s National Health Service (NHS) was among the casualties. NHS England estimated that more than 19,000 appointments would have been cancelled in total. The disruption reached hospitals and patients, showing how a technical flaw can become a public-service emergency.

Microsoft had already released a security update. But a patch cannot protect a hospital computer that has not received it.

Later in 2017, Equifax, a major American credit-reporting agency, suffered a breach affecting approximately 148m people. Attackers exploited a known Apache Struts web-application vulnerability. A fix existed, but the affected system was not secured in time.

Other incidents exposed weaknesses in technologies trusted to control access.

A flaw disclosed in 2019 in Citrix ADC and Gateway was exploited in 2020, threatening remote access. Zerologon, disclosed in 2020, could let an attacker with network access compromise a Windows domain controller managing identities. In 2021, ProxyLogon attacks exploited Microsoft Exchange email-server weaknesses, sometimes leaving attackers with persistent access.

Systems meant to connect or protect an organization could themselves become entry points.

Then came Log4Shell in Dec 2021. It received the maximum severity score of 10 out of 10. That reflected how technically serious the flaw was, not how much financial damage it caused.

Log4Shell affected Log4j, which many Java applications use to record activity. Under vulnerable conditions, specially crafted input could trigger malicious code.

Log4j could sit inside another software product much like an ingredient inside packaged food. An organization might know the product it purchased without knowing every component inside it. The risk was particularly insidious: a business could be exposed through code it had never knowingly selected.

For many, the first challenge was discovering their exposure.

The lesson applies to PHP2Shell: an office may know its website but not every component installed by its developer, host or contractor.

In 2023, MOVEit Transfer exposed another dependence. Attackers exploited file-transfer software to steal information from organizations whose suppliers used it.

A supplier’s weakness had become somebody else’s problem.

Also in 2023, CitrixBleed exposed session information in certain remote-access products. Stolen tokens could let attackers impersonate legitimate users, potentially bypassing multifactor authentication.

A patch was not necessarily the end of the response: organizations also had to investigate whether attackers had already gained access.

These are not history’s 10 worst vulnerabilities. The software changed. The recurring failures did not. A flaw becomes a crisis when software goes unnoticed, patches fail to reach systems, responsibility is unclear or attackers arrive before the fix.

Nepal has not merely watched these crises from afar. It has experienced serious cyber incidents of its own.

In 2017, WannaCry reportedly affected around 80–90 computers at a Nepali financial institution. That year, attackers compromised NIC Asia Bank’s SWIFT environment and issued fraudulent international transfer instructions. In Sept 2026, reported ransomware at a shared data centre serving 72 brokerage firms contributed to a suspension of stock-exchange trading.

The consequences ranged from infected computers and fraudulent transfer instructions to interrupted markets. Stolen credentials and other compromised data can also circulate through dark-web markets long after an incident, reinforcing the need for continued monitoring. PHP2Shell did not arrive in a country new to cyber risk. The more revealing question is whether each incident leaves Nepal better prepared for the next one.

Google’s researchers have also demonstrated AI-assisted discovery of previously unknown software vulnerabilities.

PHP2Shell brought responsibility into sharp focus. Thousands of government websites on the shared Government Integrated Website Management System (GIWMS) were patched centrally, while others depended on individual offices or vendors and took longer to restore.

Knowing who maintains a system can matter almost as much as knowing how to patch it. Clear ownership creates accountability for identifying exposure, fixing it and confirming services are safe to restore.

When a flaw threatens thousands of systems, someone must coordinate warnings and responses. India's national Computer Emergency Response Team, CERT-In, has operated since 2004. Nepal developed community initiatives, including npCERT in 2016, before establishing its government-led National Cyber Security Centre in 2024.

The roughly two-decade gap between India’s national CERT and Nepal’s government-led centre is notable, although establishment dates alone do not measure capability. What matters is whether warnings reach those who must act.

Nepal’s National Cyber Security Centre issued a PHP2Shell advisory on Oct 22. That precautionary response was encouraging, but an advisory is only the beginning: agencies must identify exposure, patch systems, check for earlier exploitation and restore services safely. Public technical accounts of some earlier incidents remain limited, although that does not mean investigations were not conducted. What matters is what happens after the warning.

Expertise must reach beyond government and Kathmandu. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP), an international software-security community, has a Kathmandu chapter; similar networks could take root in other regional centres. Universities can build expertise through research into secure software, vulnerabilities and malware.

Electricity networks, connected vehicles and drones depend on software. So do industrial-control systems such as SCADA, which monitor and control physical processes. Cybersecurity and physical security increasingly overlap.

PHP2Shell does not prove Nepal unprepared. Its precautionary response showed capacity; the question is whether readiness extends across essential services and suppliers.

What would greater readiness look like?

Start by knowing what software and components an organization runs. Developers can use the OWASP Top 10 for web-application risks and MITRE’s CWE Top 25 for dangerous software weaknesses. Independent vulnerability assessments and penetration testing can expose problems before attackers do.

Researchers need authorized reporting channels. Clear vulnerability-disclosure programs and carefully scoped bug bounties can encourage responsible reporting.

Microsoft’s monthly Patch Tuesday illustrates why updating should be routine, not improvised during a crisis. Critical or actively exploited flaws, however, cannot always wait for the next cycle.

Fixes must be verified, and possible earlier intrusion investigated. Multifactor authentication helps against account attacks but cannot repair a flaw allowing code execution without login. Updated antivirus and endpoint protection can detect or block malicious activity, but organizations also need monitoring, tested backups and rehearsed recovery plans. Prevention will sometimes fail, so an organization must be able to detect an intrusion and recover operations rather than merely reinstall software.

Software is only one route for criminals. Sometimes exploiting trust is easier than exploiting code.

The FBI documented North Korean actors posing as recruiters and sending a malicious pre-employment test to an employee of a cryptocurrency-wallet software company. Even technical experience cannot eliminate deception.

Citizens face similar risks. Following Nepal’s Aug 2026 floods, police warned about fraudulent relief appeals, fake QR codes and phishing links. Emergencies make urgency and generosity targets. An apparently helpful donation request can therefore become the entry point for fraud.

Warnings must reach professionals and ordinary citizens quickly, in languages they understand.

PHP2Shell showed the value of precaution—and of knowing which systems exist, who maintains them and how quickly they can be secured.

The next serious flaw may emerge in software few organizations realize they use. Nepal cannot predict its name or date, but it can strengthen the expertise, institutions and operational discipline needed to respond without unnecessary disruption. The next vulnerability is inevitable. The next crisis need not be.

The author is an Ireland-based cybersecurity professional and writer
